chapter: The Latin scene and business of the 1940s-70s
title: Playing with Charlie Parker
summary: Parker was powerful and not bothered by the rhythm.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Who did you enjoy playing with, parti-
larly? Who did you enjoy particularly playing with? Talk about the people you particularly --
Parker?
Well, talk about Parker and the others.
(Unintelligible.)
What was he like to work with?

I don't know, he was such a powerful man. And the funny part about it, he played (unintelligible) when they called it progressive jazz. (Unintelligible) so good, and the rhythm, he used to take that thing and just put it --
Did you ever record with him?
No.
No.
No, the guy died.
Yeah, so that was the end of that.

That was the end of -- that was my main thing. I said, this is it, this caught on fire. Because the other people that were trying to play (unintelligible). And this guy started building it and building it, with that rhythm and everything he played right on top of the (unintelligible) going and going, it was ______. That was for me one of the best guys that I had the opportunity to mix his music with my music. Charlie, naturally, and ______. I don't have to tell you about that. They're in a class by themselves.
They created something else. That was the evolution of the jazz, for good or for bad.

Do you know, it's been said, though, that Parker, Charlie, playing with Latin -- with Cuban rhythms, right? -- despite his role as a creator in jazz, played kind of inflexible. I've heard some of his recordings, and he seemed sometimes just to ignore what's going on around him, and play straight Parker in a way that Gillespie never did.

You're right about that. He knew all about what he was playing. He said to me, man, don't worry about it. When my time comes for me to start, just give me the sign and I start. So nothing bothered him. Nothing bothered him entirely. Different with Dizzy. Dizzy was on the rhythm you played. They played two different things.

This is hard to say. Some people tried to tell me Parker created his style. I say, I don't think so because I'll tell you, I made this in 1933, '34, and to me, this was great then, the same thing. The only thing that people -- they don't understand it and they (unintelligible) preparing for all the different changes that he used to make, they say he was going out of key and all that different stuff.
But to me, it was the same thing and I had a hell of a time to convince people what he was trying to do.
Yeah, I remember you talking about that.
How about other -- okay, you say Dexter, Dexter Gordon was one of the exciting people you played with, right?
Uh-huh.
On the African and jazz side. Who else?
Nobody else. (Unintelligible.) No.
To create that much emotion, nobody, nobody, nobody, not til today. And the second guy, I mention a guy, he got no name, maybe the people will laugh at me, but the only guy that can produce a --
(End of Side One.)
